Dyed
DIDE
adjective, participle
From the Saxon deagan, “to colour,” from deag, a dye — to strike a colour into a fibre so that it becomes the fibre’s own and cannot be rinsed away.

Biblical Definition

To dye is to drive colour into a fibre until it is no longer a coating but a property of the thread. Scripture uses the word in three settings, and each turns on that permanence. In the tabernacle, the LORD calls for “rams' skins dyed red” (Exo 25:5) as a covering for the tent, laid beneath the badgers' skins where no worshipper could see them (Exo 26:14). The house of God was roofed in red, and the red was hidden — the blood-covering that shelters the holy place is not for display. In Ezekiel, dyed attire is the mark of seduction: the Chaldean princes portrayed upon the wall, girded and “exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads” (Eze 23:15), a splendour painted to be lusted after. And in Isaiah the dye is on the Conqueror Himself: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa 63:1). The answer comes back, “I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save,” and the chapter tells us what dyed those garments — He trod the winepress alone, and the blood of His enemies is sprinkled upon His raiment. The whole Bible’s colour theology stands in that image: red struck permanently into cloth, whether as covering, as temptation, or as the livery of judgment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Stained or coloured by dye, so that the colour becomes proper to the fibre; in Scripture the red covering of the tabernacle and the stained garments of the Conqueror from Bozrah.

DYED, pp. [Sax. deagan, to colour, from deag, a dye.] Stained; coloured; having a colour struck into the substance.

Distinguished from painting or staining the surface: the dye enters the fibre and becomes proper to it.

The fastest ancient dyes were the scarlet of the kermes insect and the purple of the murex, both prized for permanence.

Rams' skins dyed red formed the third covering of the tabernacle (Exo 25:5; 26:14; 36:19; 39:34).

Dyed attire, in Eze 23:15, denotes the coloured headdress of the Babylonian princes.

Key Scripture

Exo 25:5 — "And rams' skins dyed red, and badgers' skins, and shittim wood,"

Exo 26:14 — "And thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins."

Isa 63:1 — "Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save."

Eze 23:15 — "Girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity:"

Modern Corruption

No party is redefining the word; what is commonly lost is that Isa 63 is a judgment oracle, softened by preachers into a picture of the Saviour stained with His own blood at Calvary.

expand to see more

Isa 63:1-6 is regularly preached as a Passion text: the Man from Edom in dyed garments is taken for Christ crimsoned with His own wounds, and the winepress is read as the cross. The instinct is devout and the reading is wrong, and the passage says so in plain words. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments.” Their blood. The dye is the blood of His enemies, not His own; the day is the day of vengeance in His heart; and Revelation takes up the same figure for the rider on the white horse who treads the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God. Softening it does not make Christ kinder, it makes Him smaller, and it robs the afflicted church of the very comfort the oracle was given to supply — that there is a day appointed when the Lamb rises as Judge and the account of Edom is settled by His own hand.

Hold the two dyed cloths together and the doctrine is whole. Under the tabernacle roof lay rams' skins dyed red, unseen by any worshipper, silently covering the house where God met His people — atonement made, and made out of sight, so that the man who came with his offering was sheltered by a red he never looked at. Over Edom comes the Conqueror in garments dyed with the blood of His foes. The same Christ is both coverings: red beneath for those who are His, red upon Him against those who are not. There is no third option and no neutral ground, for every man is either under the covering or in front of the winepress. That is why the ram’s skin was dyed and not merely painted: what God does in atonement and in judgment alike goes all the way into the fibre and never washes out.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Colour struck permanently into the fibre — the hidden red roof of the tabernacle and the stained garments of the Conqueror from Bozrah.

expand to see more

Dyed — Saxon deagan, to colour; deag, a dye.

Hebrew 'adam, to be red, in the phrase “rams' skins dyed red” (me'oddamim).

The tabernacle’s third covering, laid under the badgers' skins and seen by none (Exo 26:14).

Isa 63:1 — garments dyed from Bozrah in Edom, the blood being the enemies’ own (Isa 63:3).

Eze 23:15 — dyed attire as the painted splendour that drew Aholibah into idolatry.

Usage

"A dye enters the fibre; a paint sits on it — which is why Scripture chose dye for what cannot be undone."

"The tabernacle was roofed in red that no worshipper ever saw: atonement made, not displayed."

"Isa 63 is vengeance, not Calvary — the blood on those garments belongs to Edom."
